utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's for the Prosecution to open this part of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, today we're represented, as you see, by the Prosecutor herself, by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, and by Mr. Groome, and of course by myself. The Prosecutor will make some opening remarks and then I'll make a rather short opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Prosecutor. MS. DEL PONTE: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I will not take up much of your time this morning. Neither will Mr. Nice. I shall limit myself in a matter of minutes to a few procedural and logistical issues that have been and will continue to be of special relevance to this case. Last February, I pointed out that this trial was going to put international humanitarian law and its practice to the test. The test has obviously been conclusive in many respects. The procedural feasibility of such a trial has been established. The Prosecution presented its case for Kosovo in 110 hours, or the equivalent of five normal trial weeks. This achievement testifies to the Prosecution's commitment to an efficient administration of justice manifested in its active contribution to the search for creative solutions in trial management. However, a trial before an international forum is inconceivable without the cooperation of states. It is in this field that the fate of the trial will ultimately be played out. And unlike domestic jurisdictions, international justice has no means of enforcement. Yet state cooperation, in particular cooperation from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, is far from being exhaustive. Admittedly, during the initial stage of these proceedings Yugoslavia made it possible to hear several deposition witnesses and facilitated access to some sources of evidence material. Cooperation remains, however, fractious, difficult, unpredictable. More importantly and much to my regret, it does not appear to be guided by the will or the interest to actively participate in establishing the truth. With regard to the segment of the trial opening today, Yugoslavia continues to hold the key to irreplaceable evidence, such as potential witnesses who will need state authorisation to travel and testify, or civilian and military archives, access to which is still denied to date. I have given up the hope of seeing Belgrade encourage potential witnesses to come and testify. The only thing I ask is that they allow them to come while lifting the threat of criminal prosecution for violation of state or military secrets. As you can see, a great deal will depend on the extent to which third parties, including but not limited to Yugoslavia, will comply with their legal obligations before the Tribunal. Allow me to underscore that cooperation should not be limited to strict compliance with our requests. States and international organisations should, in my view, contribute actively to ascertaining the facts by submitting to the Trial Chamber all the evidence they know to be relevant to the case. Furthermore, administration of justice must be transparent. Public hearings must remain the rule, closed sessions the exception, justified only by the prevailing need to protect the identity of witnesses in danger. This very much coincides with the views of the Trial Chamber. A transparent administration of justice is a fundamental component of the rule of law. We therefore call upon all countries in a position to make witnesses available to us, to acknowledge and apply to international justice the principles they hold dear in their own country. In this respect, we should recall that the Trial Chamber expressed time and time again its willingness to take into consideration legitimate state interests by approving closed sessions as required to protect confidential and classified evidence. The efficiency with which the Kosovo case was led is due to a large extent to the cooperation and support of the Victims and Witnesses Section and, above all, to the witnesses' courage, willingness, and self-effacement. Given the magnitude of the trial, the fact that the Trial Chamber heard witnesses without interruption, with the exception of one 20-minute delay, is remarkable enough in view of the many imponderables and factors beyond our control. I want to pay tribute to the witnesses for their flexibility and their goodwill. Some had to extend their stay in The Hague by several days when hearings were adjourned for unexpected reasons. We do not know whether we can maintain this level of procedural efficiency in the case starting today. The cases are different. There will be fewer factual witnesses as opposed to witnesses testifying to the responsibility of the accused, who will be less flexible in terms of availability. This may well render our job a little more difficult. The Trial Chamber may, however, rest assured of our continued efforts to ensure that evidence is led without interruption. I now give the floor, with your leave, to Mr. Nice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was the accused who wanted there to be opening speeches. We drew to your attention that, of course, there have been detailed indictments, an earlier detailed opening, and a very detailed pre-trial brief to which the accused is in a position to respond. And accordingly, with an eye to who is our proper audience, this opening can be brief. Our proper audience is, of course, Your Honours, not the wider public. These proceedings are in public in order that the public can see our work is done properly, as the Prosecutor has so rightly reminded us. They're not here to provide copy, or particularly good copy for newspapers or matters of that sort. Accordingly, in this opening, I shall simply remind the Chamber of the events of these two indictments and of how we put our case, show you a few maps which I hope will be helpful in filling out the picture. At the end, I will return to say one or two things about the trial process. We already have quite a lot of evidence about events generally from evidence given in the Kosovo-only part of the trial. The break-up of the former Yugoslavia with the development of nationalism in various forms is well known to the Chamber. In the early stages, Serbs for the most part taking or expressing the position that the former Yugoslavia should dissolve, if at all, into component ethnic groups; that is, Serbs, Croats, and other groups officially recognised, not, of course, Kosovars. I trust the Chamber has been given folders of maps, and if the usher would be so good as to place the first map on the overhead projector. I, of course, don't ask for these to be produced at the moment - they will be produced in due course - these are documents simply for assistance. The first map which is from, indeed, the Times map of the Balkans, and a map with a rather complicated legend we can see on the left-hand side, breaking the inhabitants into nations and national minorities, the various colours for Croats, Macedonians, Montenegrins, striped according to the percentage by which particular areas they occupied territory, shows just how varied a place it was in population terms. We needn't look at it in detail. It tells a story visually. The idea of reformulating this pattern of occupation into one where ethnic groups could be all together is an idea that was always going to be extremely hard to achieve in any peaceful way. Hard; impossible. We turn from that map. We can leave it there for the time being until the next one is placed on the overhead projector. The Prosecution case is that the Serbs plan conceived, as plans can be without people sitting round a table with a leader telling them when their plan should be, reduced to a Serb claim to a huge expanse of the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Their plan was packaged, initially in any event, in terms of wanting people to remain in Yugoslavia, although that phrase, the Prosecution say, was or became a cover for the desire to create a Serb state. Before we move on through the events of these two indictments, the Croatian and the Bosnian indictment we are about to try, a word of resistance to temptation: There may be a temptation to characterise this accused simply as the sole architect, and that temptation may have to be resisted until the precise outlines of his role are etched by evidence, because plans can emerge without a single originator. Such plans can be joined, and there can be those who choose to lead such plans, once they join them, being criminally opportunistic and coming to be seen as and indeed to be central to the plan itself. And this may be a reality of this accused's personal history, he being a man to whom others committed to the plan looked for leadership that he was able to provide. Let's turn to Croatia in more detail. It left the communist fold in May of 1990. It suffered some rebellion in the area known as the Croat Krajina in August of 1990. We will hear evidence of how about this time Jovica Stanisic and Frenki Simatovic, names familiar to Your Honours, and others, spent time in the area arming, training, and organising the local Serb police and armed groups in cooperation with a man called Milan Martic of whom you will be familiar, and of others. We come to early 1991, and in March, as will be dealt with by Mr. Mesic, the present President of Croatia next week, in Karadjordjevo there was, there may be no doubt, an agreement between this accused and President Tudjman of Croatia to carve up Bosnia, a plan that was afoot quite without prejudice to the Croatian war into which those two men were to engage. At the same sort of time, there was Karadzic, leader of the Bosnian SDS party who shared Milosevic's goal, being recorded as saying such things as, "It is as natural as rain falls that the Serbs should live in the same state." On the 15th of March, of 1991, this accused announced that the Presidency of Yugoslavia no longer existed, and indeed in a meeting then secret of local government leaders, revealed what was in his mind when he said, "It is always the powerful and never the weak who dictate frontiers. He also said that Serbia would no longer be bound by decisions of the Federal Presidency, the rump of which he was soon himself to control. The war covered by the Croatian indictment starts really in August of 1991, the accused being President of Serbia, the federal institutions being really only nominally intact. And we will discover that Kadijevic, the Federal Secretary of Defence was a man already being seen to be responsive to the accused, who as I say was but President of Serbia, and although he may have had no formal authority over the army at that time, he was able to exert some effective control. And these mechanisms of control reveal the beginning of the new order. First blood of this war really in the spring of 1991 between Croatian police and rebel Serbs, with interventions by the JNA supporting the Serbs and not the Yugoslav contention, the accused himself pressing that the army should pursue the Serb cause whatever public stance he might have taken. His public statements being already aimed at deflecting international condemnation. This deception was very important, as it was important that Serbian participation in the war should be concealed, something we shall discover acknowledged by some Serb leaders at that very time in unguarded moments. And that may be why so much was done by this accused through proxies, such as the Federal Presidency or Rump Presidency itself, or through other leaders in Knin and elsewhere who could be directed, encouraged, supplied, but then publicly disavowed. Mr. Mesic, as I say now President Mesic, was due for appointment or election to the rotating Presidency of the former Yugoslavia, and his appointment was effectively blocked for several months, between May and July, when he was only grudgingly allowed into office that he was only able to exercise effectively for a few months, until September. May we now then look at a map that shows the ethnic distribution of Croatia; map 2. I'm not sure that the colours on the various maps that I shall provide to you for your assistance are all consistent, but you will see here red for dominance by Serbs, yellow for Croatians. And what is, of course, remarkable or notable is that towards the west there are areas -- I beg your pardon. To the west of the overall map but to the east of the centre of Croatia there are areas strongly red. Further to the east, although there is by the different strengths of shading some Serb presence, you will see nothing of great strength at all; no clear majorities, just some mixed communities and many communities with, as one would expect, a Croatian majority. Leaving that map on the overhead projector the account is as follows as what happened: In early August, the JNA began to take over Baranja in Eastern Slavonia - it's up in the northeastern corner of the map - while stepping up attacks on Croat villages in that area. There was a Croat plurality in those areas only. Not only; there was a Croat plurality, more Croats than others. But the JNA handed over control to local Serbs, ultimately led by the man Goran Hadzic, and a campaign of terror began, reflected in the indictment, involving arbitrary arrests and detentions, mass killings, expulsions, destruction of property carried out by paramilitaries, by local Serb forces and, in some cases, by the JNA itself. So we have the development of the picture of combined forces operating together. And those paramilitaries, part of that combined force, will be shown to have had close ties to the MUP of Serbia, to close associates of the accused whom he would continue to support for years, and indeed to the accused himself. Now, the Croats blockaded the JNA barracks in Croatia in mid-September. This may be relied upon as some explanation for some of what followed. What followed was that the JNA from elsewhere, together with local Serbs, struck in five directions aimed at the dismemberment and total defeat of Croatia, although that objective of the JNA's may not have been at that time the particular objective of the accused whose different interest I have already identified and summarised. Can we now place map 3 on the overhead projector. This reveals the SAOs, the Serb autonomous regions, that were declared. But I use the map at this stage for a different purpose. Although it doesn't have the characteristic arrows on it, the Court will hear in due course how at this time attacks from Serbia were mounted into East Slavonia. That is the etched area on the right-hand side which of course includes Vukovar. Attacks were mounted south from Bosnia moving north into West Slavonia, the middle of the etched areas. There was an intention, it would appear, to cut the access roads into West Slavonia. There were attacks mounted west out of Bosnia towards the Slovenian border, and those were aimed at separating Zagreb from the coast. Then to the south and west on this map, there were attacks from Knin to Zadar and Sibenik nearer to the coast aimed at the coast and to split Dalmatia. And Your Honours will see Skabrnje marked along with Nadin, to which I'll refer in a second. Finally, and not marked but Your Honours will know the geography, from Montenegro and Eastern Herzegovina, there were the attacks on Dubrovnik. Skabrnje near Zadar, we can see. Just an incident of significance. Ratko Mladic, Chief of Staff of the 9th corps of the JNA, carried out a threat he made on his own terms to destroy those two villages there, without justification murdering 45 elderly Croats and some other 26 to die in the following months. He was then, of course, commander of the supposedly neutral JNA, but he and Milan Martic, commander of the rebel Serb militia who was also involved in these crimes, spoke publicly of their full cooperation and integration, one with another. Those two men, Mladic and Martic, later to benefit from decisions made by this accused and others. He was involved in the decisions. Mladic to become the Bosnian Serb commander, Martic to become the Croatian Serb political chief. Approval of men whose acts must already have been known. Dubrovnik, a town with few if any legal targets, shelled about 1.000 times for no discernible reason save intimidation or reprisal. There and in the area, over 40 civilians killed. And the Chamber will have to decide in due course whether these attacks could conceivably be justified or whether they were, through disproportionality, recklessness or simple intent, as alleged, criminal acts for which this accused bears responsibility. Vukovar in Eastern Slavonia, at the top of your plans and maps, destroyed with massive loss of life, followed by the awful event where the hospital was emptied and between 200 and 300 men from that hospital executed. Vukovar perhaps an example of how, over time, the JNA made the fateful decision to collaborate with or to incorporate what were called volunteers, often men with no business serving in the army at all, or paramilitaries such as Arkan. Now, the limitations of time quite appropriate and proper for a case like this lead to a selection of charges that we must be careful do not give any incorrect impression. Vukovar and Dubrovnik are towns - cities - identified as under attack, but there were others, and that should be remembered; Zadar, Osijek, Vinkovci in East Slavonia, and other smaller towns similarly. The major and the notorious events - for example, Vukovar - should not obscure the fact that villages in these areas and the area of Dubrovnik even, were plundered and destroyed with the populations fleeing. And their stories, although they may not be before you in great detail, their accounts should not be overlooked. There was, of course, no conceivable reason for gangs, criminal gangs like Arkan's, to be involved in the way they were in this war. Groups that had, as the evidence will reveal, continuing support from the accused, indicative, indeed, of criminal intent. And there can be no doubt, as a witness at a meeting with Cyrus Vance will reveal, there can be no doubt that this accused was confronted in the strongest terms with the detail of what Arkan did. In September, while this assault was being perpetrated, the Bosnian Serbs were themselves establishing autonomous districts covering most of Bosnia, similar to what the Serbs had done. At this stage, you will hear of the degree of contact between this accused and those Bosnian Serbs. As we move in this summary from or to the time when I shall leave Croatia, it may be worth having in mind this: that many of the worst crimes in Croatia happened either sometimes near the end of combat but certainly quite unrelated to military roles and were pure crime. The Vukovar Hospital, the Vocin massacre on the day of the Serb withdrawal, the killings of the elderly in Skabrnje after a ceasefire, and the very worst of the shelling in Dubrovnik which happened on the day before the ceasefire. We reach October 1991, a bad and significant month where patterns may be discerned, patterns that inevitably speak of a plan. The JNA had started to incorporate volunteers of the type I've already described, began cooperating closely with Arkan, and around Dubrovnik we will find officers of the JNA not only tolerating but leading the plunder and destruction of village after village while indiscriminate shelling was claiming lives. At the same sort of time, in Bosnia, any appearance of real peace may have been deceptive, for intercepted telephone calls will show the full involvement of the Bosnian Serb leadership in the Croatian war: sending volunteers and recruits, touring the front lines, the Bosnian SDS party finalising its plans for seizing power and imposing ethnic separation, Karadzic warning that Muslims would disappear. And we will hear of documentary evidence, or see documentary evidence, showing that the Serb preparation for taking power was at the same time a preparation for ethnic separation, something, as we perhaps can imagine and will see most clearly from a map, inconceivable without large movements of population. In Belgrade, the Serbian bloc abandoned legality and seized control of effective power under, effectively, this accused as, for example, Mr. Mesic will say. And a pattern will develop of activities on the ground, both in Croatia and then Bosnia, with which the Chamber will already be familiar from what happened in Kosovo years later. A pattern of Serb forces surrounding and shelling villages, often that being the JNA; entry of the villages often by Territorial Defence, police, or paramilitaries, killing sometimes a few, sometimes many; terror tactics to drive out the unwanted population, expelling survivors, looting homes, and destroying what was left with explosives and fire; an overall process operated as if a single weapon achieving a single objective greater and worse than the individual and component killings or other acts. And the issue, of course, for this Trial Chamber is who was able to operate this weapon? Who influenced its operation, both for this indictment and of course at the other material times? The Prosecution say that the systematic and organised way in which attacks against non-Serb civilian populations in Croatia were carried out revealed a carefully designed scheme and strategy within an overall plan that may be laid at the door of this accused. May we look at map 4, please. The ambitions of the Serbs in Croatia were not entirely realised. This map shows in blue the declared independent areas but in red the areas that they in fact were successful in occupying. In Bosnia, we will see we have census material that goes to show the degree of success of the Bosnian Serbs' operations. We have no such census material for the post-war effects in Croatia because by the time any other census was held, people had moved back. But this map gives an idea of the degree to which they were successful in changing the ethnic balance. Can we turn now to map 5 and to Bosnia. A similar system of legend with colours showing ethnic majorities: Red for Serbs, green for Muslims, and blue for Croats, with intermediate colours representing areas where there were no clear majorities. A very varied map. The top map, if we can just focus on that, shows the position in 1991. And if the usher would be good enough to lay the transparency on top of it, please, which you don't have in your papers I'm afraid, I have it here. This is a transparency which repeats what we were able to see on map 2. And the transparency can be available to the Court at any time it wants to see it. We can see the overall composition of ethnic groups at the beginning of 1991. And what's clear, apart from the absolute variety of composition, is that although there is a large Serb area west or centre of the plan, there's no connection of Serb majority areas between that area and Serbia itself. Indeed, there's the gap at the top, when you put both maps together, still a gap in which, of course, features Brcko. Further, if you look at the eastern border of this combined map of Croatia and Bosnia, the eastern border, you can see an area of green; clear Muslim majority. No suggestion, none could ever be made, that the residents of those eastern areas, any more perhaps than those of the area that lay between the western and eastern parts coloured in red at the top, had any desire to leave their territory. So that's the picture of Bosnia with Croatia. We can take the overhead -- the transparency off now. Thank you. That's the overall picture. This, then, the picture of Bosnia itself. The crimes under the Statute charged in respect of the accused's involvement in Bosnia of course include genocide, contrary to Article 4. A crime that needs careful handling, for it creates strong emotions, is regarded as possessed in the language of sufferers of grave crimes, whether those crimes are genocide or not, and a crime that it has to be borne in mind may sometimes be less serious in terms of human suffering than crimes that cannot be categorised as genocide, and thus it's our duty as Prosecutors to keep the most careful and watchful eye on the evidence available to prove genocide, to have an eye to the law related to it. And it will be for the Chamber to decide in due course whether the offences charged here were, as the Prosecution asserts, crimes of genocide insofar as that is charged or whether this is persecution by destruction of individuals. But I repeat, in fact in terms of comparative human gravity, there is no guarantee that one crime or the other will always and necessarily be the worst. But we will submit at the conclusion of the evidence that the accused intended to destroy the Bosnian Muslim community in part in order to fulfil the aims of the objective of the criminal enterprise where prosecutions would be insufficient to achieve the desired result, or alternatively, that genocide was the natural and foreseeable consequence of the joint criminal enterprise, forcibly and permanently to remove non-Serbs from territory, or that the accused was an accomplice in that he knew that some of the principal perpetrators were committing genocide and he took or undertook acts to assist in their commission. And of course, as the Chamber will recognise, an alternative approach under 7(3) of the Statute is that, as a superior, he knew or had reason to know that genocide was about to be committed or had been committed and he took no steps to prevent or punish the perpetrators. In all cases, this accused had an influential role over other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. members of the joint criminal enterprise identified, of course, in the indictment. And he used his control and influence over elements of the JNA, or the VJ as it was to become, and the MUP, over individual politicians and over the political and military leadership of the Republika Srpska as that was, in due course, to be declared. In all cases he utilised the many resources at his disposal to ensure efficient execution of the schemes designed to achieve the overall plan. He had a fundamental role in the planning, the organisation, the financing, the direction of the plan. He was thus an essential participant in the criminal enterprise to the extent that, without him, it is hard to conceive of the enterprise or enterprises happening. Briefly the facts and the crimes charged. The autonomous areas here, which we'll see on a map in a few minutes, were declared in September 1991 but are probably less significant or certainly less significant here than the particular municipalities of which you will hear detailed evidence. The pattern of events in all municipalities was similar. In some, the non-Serbs were so cowed that they offered no resistance and the Serbs were simply able to seize control. In others, there was resistance, often quite weak, where Serb forces, the JNA and paramilitary forces with special units of the Serb MUP and units of Bosnian Serbs working as one could attack with criminal disregard for civilian life. And in all these varieties, with or without resistance, the population was faced with expulsion, imprisonment in inhumane conditions, frequently of those holding key positions in local communities, torture, sexual assaults, killings in small or large numbers and with collateral effects, finding themselves sometimes compelled to wear armbands for not being Serbs, facing other persecutions, facing loss of jobs, seeing their mosques and their churches destroyed. Factors significant for the accused's involvement include that in some areas the participation of forces and individuals were closely associated with or subordinated to the accused or to his inner circle. In other areas, the Prosecution will argue that the accused incurred liability through his participation in the joint criminal enterprise of which these acts were a consequence. While we have the map in front of us, can I turn to two particular groups of municipalities that comprise perhaps the bulk of those the Prosecution intends to deal with in detail. It may actually be helpful if I invite you to look, at this stage, at the next map. It may be out of order, but can we look at map 6, please. While that's going on the overhead projector, the Chamber will recall that originally some 47 municipalities were charged. And again, for reasons of absolutely proper judicial economy, decisions have been made only to deal in detail with certain municipalities, to deal in much less detail with another number of municipalities, and finally, for there to be a third category where only demographic evidence will be presented. The map now on the overhead projector shows that plan of ours. The strong blue colour is in respect of the municipalities, primary municipalities as we've described them, where full evidence will be given. The lighter blue but solid colour represents those for which evidence will be presented on selected egregious crimes and in respect of matters that link to the accused. The municipalities with vertical stripes are those where only demographic evidence will be presented. So the Chamber will see that the selection provides a spread - we hope a fair spread - but covers, and I now turn to these two particular groups of municipalities, the Drina Valley in the east. I spoke of the SAOs and said that they were of less importance. It may be valuable for the Chamber for reference purposes to have a knowledge of what were the declared SAOs, and you can see them here; the Krajina, Northern Bosnia, Semberija, Romania, Birac, and Herzegovina. And for what it's worth, the Chamber will observe that in the west, Bihac was not even within a declared area. And as we come to it, those municipalities in the Drina Valley or some of them - Zvornik, Bratunac, Srebrenica and Visegrad - scenes of some of the worst crimes, were also not in any declared municipality, but then the Chamber will recall from map 5 that they were, of course, areas without any Serb majority. In the Drina Valley, starting at Bijeljina, Zvornik, Bratunac, Srebrenica and Visegrad, we discover municipalities that had this in common: Serb minority except possibly in Bijeljina where it was known - and there was a map produced by the accused's own party in January 1992 that shows this - it's clear that these areas had no interest in joining a Serb state, whether called Yugoslavia or under any other name. They were all taken early in the war, and they were all taken with the participation of many forces from Serbia with close links to the accused and his inner circle, such as Arkan. They were taken by elements of the JNA commanded by individuals such as Ojdanic or by agents of the Serbian police DB, and special forces of the Serbian MUP and other paramilitary forces from Serbia.

utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what's the total number of municipalities on which evidence other than demographic evidence will be presented?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The current, as our list reveals, the current total is of 14 municipalities strong blue, 24 municipalities paler blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Out of?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forty-seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Forty-seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But, of course, in the paler blue colours, it's only individual pieces of material evidence that we will lay before you. And incidentally, although we have had - for which we are grateful - a month's pause before the time when we must make further and give further consideration to and make further adjustment to the indictments, there may be further reductions. Returning to the Drina Valley municipalities, most or all were the scenes of mass executions or mass expulsions. They were places where authority was handed to the SDS party. They were places where crimes were heavily reported by international officials and the international press so thus brought to the attention of the accused. Visegrad itself saw paramilitaries from Serbia, mass killings, people being burned alive, and indeed saw, at one stage, Colonel Jovanovic addressing a group of several thousand Muslims gathered in the football stadium, informing them that the widely feared White Eagles were there under his command. The forces had entered the town in the face of rising tension, it has to be accepted, between the Serbs and Muslims because of something that the Muslims had done. But the Prosecution say the gravest crimes were committed. Bosanski Samac, elsewhere on this map, on the left, taken over by special forces of the Serbian MUP on the 17th of April under the overall command of Simatovic with local Serb police and the JNA involved, saw the local SDS installed as the authority, imposing a regime of egregious persecutions and armbands to be worn by non-Serbs, with mass detentions and killings. That's over in the Krajina. Brcko, the area to which I referred earlier as being between any Serb-dominated areas, indeed an area of Muslim plurality, was attacked by mixed Serb forces including paramilitaries, with local Serb units and JNA members, suffered ethnic cleansing and summary executions in the presence of special forces of the Serbian MUP. Western Bosnia, sometimes known as the Krajina, three adjacent municipalities targeted in what was a campaign of persecution or cleansing in the early summer of 1992. Bosanska Krupa attacked by the JNA and other Serb forces - you can see it there - with mass detentions, executions, and cleansing. Prijedor suffering mass cleansing through the summer, with men sent to the famous infamous camps of Omarska, Keraterm, Manjaca and Trnopolje, with severe abuse and mass executions. And Sanski Most, you also see a plurality of Muslims here, the JNA involved with the defence, Territorial Defence, and local police in repeated mass killings and detentions in camps, just as in Prijedor. Mass expulsion of the remaining non-Serbs with executions by Arkan and his men, Arkan now perhaps being countable as effectively part of the Serbian DB, or at least later so to be counted. Sarajevo. The accused has told the Chamber that he opposed the lengthy bombardment of Sarajevo which happened between 1992 and 1995. At the same time as he may have been publicly opposing the attack on the civilian population of Sarajevo, the VJ was paying the very officers who were in command of the forces responsible for the attack. And the Prosecution will present evidence of that financial support given to offices including, in particular, General Galic, commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from September 1992 until August 1994. These campaigns, it has to be borne in mind, and their consequences continued, the suffering continued through this armed conflict notwithstanding the presence of UNPROFOR on the territory from 1992 and until the Dayton Agreements of 1995. But of course, one cannot turn from a summary of Bosnia without some words about the safe havens or enclaves. The military campaigns by the JNA and the army of Republika Srpska in 1992 had the effect of forcing fleeing Muslim civilians into particular pockets which came to be known as safe areas; Bihac, Gorazde, Srebrenica and Zepa. Access roads being controlled by that same Bosnian Serb army. The Bosnian Serb political and military authorities adopted a policy of obstructing medical and food supplies into the enclaves, of subjecting the besieged civilians inside to indiscriminate shelling and sniping. All of which were persecutory activities designed, in the words of a VRS directive we will look at in the course of the trial -- I have available if the Chamber wants to see it now, but I'll take it shortly. In the words of a directive from Karadzic creating or to create "an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope for further survival or life of the inhabitants." Your Honours, just give me one minute, please. Humanitarian and other aid agencies are in a position to describe the intense negotiations that were conducted with the Bosnian Serb leaders and with the leaders in Serbia, including this accused, for access to the enclaves. But often even after access was granted, there would be restrictions on humanitarian aid, there would be harassment of the residents and continuing unreasonable behaviour, adding to the misery of those living there. So that the enclaves took on increasingly camp-like characteristics with large numbers of Muslims trapped in small, well-defined areas, suffering shortage of housing, living in unsanitary conditions, without food, being unable to move without indiscriminate shelling, finding their hospitals overcrowded, people suffering amputations without anaesthesia, death from infection all being commonplace. The civilian population knew that they could not escape, and as one witness observed, the impression created in the civilian population of this particular enclave was of a relentless and unstoppable momentum that could only lead to the eventual death of everyone inside. Srebrenica and Zepa were eventually taken by the VRS in the summer of 1995, the other enclaves remaining within the control of the Bosnian government throughout the war. So far as Srebrenica itself is concerned: The enclave established in 1993, attacks on Srebrenica, from time to time the VJ intervening, and it has to be accepted, there being operations from Srebrenica by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, all led in July 1995 to Karadzic and Mladic deciding to wipe it out by force, killing all the men they found. No doubt, of course, the Dutch report will be considered for admission into evidence on this topic in due course. The accused was linked to Srebrenica in two primary ways. The VJ continued its support for the VRS. We will have, for example, Krstic's, the commander's, VJ ID card found on him when he was arrested, as an exhibit.

In addition, there was supply and support. One can see, looking at the two parts of map 8, the first part on then the bottom part, the distribution of ethnic majorities as it was in 1991; green, mixed colour, red, green, and so on. If we then look at the bottom map, we can see what was achieved in turning areas that had no interest in being Serb states into maps that could be coloured red, as at 1997. So thus, therefore, what was achieved by this campaign? Ethnic cleansing; what we can see pictorially and of which we will learn about from witnesses. Your Honours, this Tribunal is, of course, not political. It doesn't need to concern itself with or to explain how it was that the accused was left to recover after Dayton, where this border was identified, as an apparently respectable member of the community. In any event, participators well knew -- participators and observers well knew what he was and what he'd been doing. And the Chamber will remember from my earlier opening what Mr. Eagleburger had said so much earlier in events: The short fact is that the crimes of this accused long revealed -- long suspected have now been revealed by evidence. And a word or so about evidence, categories of evidence, and about the trial process, and I will be done. Evidence in relation to this accused comes from various sources. And it has to be borne in mind that criminals, or politicians who do acts that are or are subsequently revealed as being criminal, don't leave traces behind them. They don't leave paper trails. That's why, of course, this accused operated in that curiously empty office, dealing with people on a one-to-one basis so that individuals could not know what was being said to the others. Maybe. For such individuals, it may be -- as this accused, it may be helpful to think of the available witnesses as coming in circles that surround him. First, there will be the close circle of people, some of whom, for example President Lilic - or ex-President Lilic, sometime President Lilic - who we will be calling, we hope, quite soon. Or Mr. Mesic. People who can be advanced to the Chamber as witnesses whose evidence will be capable of being accepted in full. But others of this close circle may be people who will have their own interests, personal or other, to serve, and who may not be inclined to tell the whole truth. And those close witnesses, particularly the ones who may have their own interests to serve, are really rather like standing stones surrounding the accused. Next out from them in the circles of witnesses, there are others; military commanders at various levels, political people at various levels, associates of one kind or another, who may be able to tell the whole truth as they saw it but whose vision of the accused will necessarily be limited, not least because it may be obscured by some of those closer to him who will want to obscure the full detail. But that next circle of witnesses will be able to provide some light on the accused. They will also be able to look out to the crimes that were committed. And then there is the outer circle of witnesses, witnesses who must be available to the Chamber, although we hope that they will be able to be taken for the most part shortly, perhaps in writing, witnesses who will deal with the crimes that were committed but who may be able to say little or nothing about the accused beyond what they say about identifying units committing crimes that may be traceable by one route or another to him. And so all those witnesses provide differing shafts of light in circumstances where it is, whatever a different audience might hope or think, unlikely that there will be an individual witness who will be able to tell the whole truth about this man. And I make that point because it is important for those watching this trial to recognise that the hard and detailed work that this Chamber has to do is the work of putting together pieces of evidence that will come from different sources. There are the internationals, there are the experts, each of whom will be able to provide but a small vision or view of the accused. It is, of course, the composition of those views that, in due course, will establish the guilt of this man. And I return to one particular point about one particular category of witnesses, those of the inner circle who may not tell the truth. Should they simply, because they may not tell the whole truth, not be called? One can imagine perhaps in any real or hypothetical case of a top leader being tried on his own, the Chamber asking itself the question: Would we rather proceed with or without hearing from witnesses so close that they might have their own, in the vernacular, fish to fry, or would we rather simply proceed without exercising our own judgement on those people? We would invite the Chamber to say that it is obviously preferable, wherever possible, to do as we have already done with one or two witnesses and to call witnesses from that inner circle. We can't know if this accused, who doesn't respect the Court, will call any evidence at all. We judge that it is wise and sensible to call as many of the inner circle as we can, confident that the Chamber will be in a position to assess, and we may be able to assist in that assessment, where the truth lies; confident that if inner circle witnesses turn up, as one may have done or be thought to have done, parrot agreement in cross-examination to propositions that were untrue, confident that those untruths can be proved. There should be no hiding place for witnesses who may prefer not to give evidence but who can, and of course morally should, provide a fuller truth for this Tribunal. "SPEAKER: German support for Croatian separatists received an unusual tribute: A musical thank you on Croatian state television. "SPEAKER: Thank you, Germany. "SPEAKER: ... public relations firm Ruder and Finn, Croatia successfully used the media to manipulate a larger audience, particularly Germany and the US, to gain support for its separatist agenda. This was particularly evident in the reporting of the war around the resort town of Dubrovnik, a favourite vacation for German tourists. Working through its Washington PR firm, the Croatian government managed to convince much of the world that Dubrovnik was being destroyed by the Serbs in unprovoked attacks which lasted for months during the fall of 1991. "SPEAKER: The public has been led to believe that the federal army attack on Dubrovnik was not precipitated by anything but sheer malice. However, on August 25th of 1991, Croatian forces attacked a base in the Bay of Kotor and the Bay of Kotor, and they were repulsed with heavy losses. "SPEAKER: Yugoslav troops based in Montenegro then fought their way up the coast, confronting Croatian forces near Dubrovnik. "SPEAKER: Targets outside the Old City were hit, consisting mostly of hotels which had been taken over as barracks and spotter points by Croatian forces. "SPEAKER: Contrary to news reports, there was little damage to the historic Old City. "SPEAKER: Yes. It has been reported some 15.000 shells rained on the Old City of Dubrovnik. I counted 15 mortar hits on the main street. The Yugoslav federal army could have destroyed the Old City of Dubrovnik in two hours. It is not destroyed. "SPEAKER: Washington Post reporter Peter Maas, who visited the Old City several months after the fighting stopped, found Dubrovnik in what he described as 'nearly pristine' condition. "SPEAKER: There are many people who go to these scenes of mayhem and adventure who don't know where they are, who don't know the languages, cannot really communicate with the people, and who take press handouts from the local authorities. So there is certainly an orchestrated effort on the part of the Croatian and Slovenia, Austrian and German media to portray the Serbs as a bunch of howling, Byzantine uncivilised barbarians. "SPEAKER: These impressions helped strengthen Germany's resolve to lead a reluctant European Community to recognise the separatist republics and thereby dismantle Yugoslavia. To overcome British opposition to recognising Croatia, German Prime Minister Helmut Kohl offered British leader John Major a deal which left Britain free to disregard or opt out of the social provisions of the 1991 treaty creating a unified Europe which was being hotly debated in the British parliament. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. This helped John Major politically at home but Bosnia would pay a high price. "The French, who needed German help to stabilise France's currency, also dropped their opposition to recognising the separatist republics. The United States, the only power strong enough to oppose Germany, began to waiver. Deputy Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger, who had once served as US Ambassador to Yugoslavia and spoke Serbo-Croat, knew well the dangers of a wider war if recognition were extended before a settlement had been reached between the different ethnic groups. "SPEAKER: I think the major lesson here is that when you get involved in something like this with a thousand years of history underlying it all, you need to understand that once the dam breaks, the viciousness can be pretty awful, on all sides. "SPEAKER: In the end, here also peace would be sacrificed for domestic politics. There was an American election coming up. "SPEAKER: When we finally went ahead and recognised, one of the reasons we did so is because it had become a major domestic political issue for us here. We have particularly a large Croatian-American community. And Mr. Bush lost most of them in the election that he lost because they were unhappy in our having delayed as long as we did in recognising Croatia. "SPEAKER: While German actions encouraged the armed secession of Slovenia and Croatia, it was US diplomacy, particularly through Ambassador Warren Zimmermann, which helped light the spark for a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina by supporting Muslim leader Alija Izetbegovic in his bid for a separate state. "SPEAKER: And then we were the ones that went to the Europeans and insisted that they recognise Bosnia and then that we would recognise all three of the new states, and that was a deal that was made, and of course, it was precisely that that led to the current war. "SPEAKER: This was a war that European leaders believe could have been avoided. "SPEAKER: The Bosnian Serbs, until comparatively recently, have been in the majority in Bosnia, and then the Muslims, who had a very much higher birth rate than the Serbs, became the predominant -- the majority population. And this, of course, was something very hard for the Serbs to swallow. And they made it abundantly plain very early on that they were not prepared to accept a situation in which there was an independent Bosnia under the constitution which then prevailed. And indeed under the constitution which then prevailed, it was not -- it was illegal for Izetbegovic to declare independence because any constitutional change of that magnitude had to be agreed by all three parties. "SPEAKER: Privately, European leaders worried about Izetbegovic's close ties to Iran and the possibility of a Muslim fundamentalist state in the heart of a newly-unified Europe. "SPEAKER: Izetbegovic himself had ties to the Iranians going back long before they came to power in Bosnia, really beginning not too long after the Iranian revolution, came to power in 1979. "SPEAKER: In his book, 'The Politics of Diplomacy' then Secretary of State James Baker wrote that Ambassador Zimmermann strongly advised him to recognise Bosnia. Recognition of Bosnia, however, violated the most basic diplomatic norms. For a government to be recognised, it must be in full control of its territory, it must have clearly established borders, it must also have a stable population. Not a single one of these essential conditions existed in Bosnia in February of 1992 when Zimmermann made his recommendation. US intelligence analysts predicted that recognition would lead to war. Even the Germans thought that recognition of Bosnia would be a serious mistake. "SPEAKER: We did have some different opinions in early 1992 as the Americans supported the recognition of Bosnia whereas we, the Europeans, believed that we should first establish a framework for the whole region. "SPEAKER: Lord Carrington tried to avert disaster by appointing Portuguese President Jose Cutilheiro to find common ground among the Serbs, Muslims and Croats before an independent Bosnia was recognised. "SPEAKER: I asked him to go to Sarajevo and to Lisbon and to have talks with the three parties in Bosnia to see whether or not some agreement could be reached with an unitary state, I mean a state, an independent Bosnian state but in some sort of federal idea in which you've got the three communities to agree. "SPEAKER: This set up a central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and three ethnic cantons, on the model of Switzerland. "SPEAKER: It was the last chance, I think, of trying to preserve Bosnia before the war broke out in earnest. "SPEAKER: If the Lisbon plan had been adopted, British author and BBC journalist Misha Glenny wrote later, 'The war in Bosnia probably would not have happened.' But two days after signing it, following a meeting with American Ambassador Warren Zimmermann, Izetbegovic changed his mind and disavowed his signature. "SPEAKER: Izetbegovic turned around and reneged, as he's reneged on other things. "SPEAKER: Zimmermann later acknowledged to David Binder of the New York Times that Izetbegovic had reluctantly signed the agreement to gain European recognition. More than a year after the bloodshed began in Bosnia, Zimmermann also admitted that the Lisbon plan was not bad at all but recalls telling Izetbegovic, 'If you don't like it, why sign it?' "SPEAKER: Zimmermann told Izetbegovic, Look, why don't you wait and see what the US can do for you, meaning we'll recognise you and then help you out. So don't go ahead with the Lisbon Agreement, don't accept the Cutilheiro plan, and just hold out for some kind of unitary Bosnian state. So this is a major turning point in our diplomatic efforts. "SPEAKER: The American administration made it quite clear that they thought that the proposals, Cutilheiro and my proposals were unacceptable. "SPEAKER: With no agreement amongst the Muslims, Serbs, and Croats with all sides mobilised for war, the European Community voted, as the US insisted, to recognise Bosnia on April 6, along with Slovenia and Croatia. This act, Roger Cohen of the New York Times later wrote, was 'as close to criminal negligence as a diplomatic act can be.' Indeed, international recognition and the outbreak of the Bosnian war were simultaneous. The world put light to the fuse. "SPEAKER: God is great. Allah Akhbar. Call for the holy war. Holy warrior. Allah-u-ekber. God is great. Holy warrior. Allah-u-ekber. God is great. "SPEAKER: ... determined that we should not take sides in this war by becoming a combatant, and we have held firmly to that position and we plan to continue to hold firmly to that position. SPEAKER: By the time US Secretary of Defence William Perry testified before Congress in June of 1995 that the US was not taking sides in the Yugoslav conflict, a full range of secret military assistance operations to the Croatian government and Bosnian Muslim forces were already underway. At a remote air field high in the mountains of the Croatian island of Brac, American intelligence operatives assembled the unmanned aviation vehicles, known as UAVs, for reconnaissance while Croatian soldiers guarded the airport grates. Only one month before Defence Secretary William Perry testified that the US was not taking sides, a predominantly Serbian civilian area, supposedly under UN protection, was suddenly attacked by Croatian forces. Several UN soldiers were killed in what turned out to be a massacre of the Serbian civilian population of Sector West. Thousands of Serbian refugees fled across the Sava River from Croatia into Northern Bosnia. Croatian sources put the number of Serbs killed in the attack at 1.000. Serbian Orthodox Church officials stated that 5.000 civilians were killed. But there is no criticism of this atrocity by American officials, including the killing of UN soldiers, because the US was deeply involved in assisting the Croatian military. Efforts by British and French representatives on the UN Security Council to place sanctions against Croatia were repeatedly blocked by America's UN representative Madeleine Albright. Six months earlier, in November of 1994, the US Departments of State and Defence had approved a contract between a group of retired four star generals and the Croatian government. "SPEAKER: The Croats paid for it but they were authorised by the Pentagon. "SPEAKER: I had constant reports of American officers who were, quote, retired, no longer on active duty, acting as advisors to the Bosnian government's military, acting as advisors to the Croatian military. And they were very active on the ground. "SPEAKER: The retired generals, described as high level mercenaries, belonged to a private company known as Military Professional Resources Incorporated, or MPRI. MPRI included such luminaries as Lieutenant General Ed Soister [phoen], former head of the Defence Intelligence Agency, Major General Richard Griffiths, Deputy Chief of Operations in Central Europe, and most importantly Karl Vuono. General Vuono and his colleagues at MPRI would be a major asset to the Croatian army in its efforts to forcibly expel the ethnic Serbian population from the Krajina, which was technically under UN protection in sectors north and south. But the destruction of Sector West, a UN protected area for ethnic Serbs, would have consequences in nearby Bosnia. Lord Owen wrote that by acquiescing in the Croatian government's seizure of Sector West, the US had, quote, in effect given the green light to the Bosnian Serbs to attack Srebrenica and Zepa. When Muslim paramilitary leader Naser Oric launched an attack from Srebrenica against the Serbian village of Visnjica, this time the surrounding Serbian forces counterattacked Srebrenica, entering the city. "SPEAKER: It is well known to anybody who has followed this that Oric was launching repeated attacks out of a supposedly demilitarised zone against surrounding Serbian areas around the Srebrenica enclave, to the point where, after repeated warnings, the Serbs simply could not allow him to continue to do that and decided to take the town. "SPEAKER: Oric and several thousand of his soldiers fled across Serbian held territory to the town of Tuzla several days before Serb forces entered Srebrenica and Zepa. Muslim women and children in Srebrenica were placed on buses by Serbian forces and sent to safety in Tuzla. But between 1 and 2.000 Muslim men were captured by the Serbs who blamed them for participating in a string of massacres led by Naser Oric. A Croatian soldier who claims to have fought with the Bosnian Serbs testified at The Hague that he took part in the execution of 1.200 Muslims, although the number of bodies recovered from the site was 200. UN [sic] Ambassador Madeleine Albright, however, used greatly inflated numbers to describe Serbian reprisals at Srebrenica. According to the International Committee of the Red Cross, thousands of Muslim men, allegedly missing, were found serving in Muslim army units near Tuzla. Washington Post reporter John Pomfritt [phoen] reported that 4.000 armed Muslim soldiers had escaped to a town near Tuzla, yet these same soldiers were still be included in official reports years later as missing Muslims from Srebrenica. "SPEAKER: Secretary Albright in particular was very insistent on using such numbers like 8.000, 10.000 Muslim men and boys who were executed in Srebrenica by the Serbs. There's simply nothing to document those numbers. "SPEAKER: ... that year whose records of fighters had killed many Serb civilians. Other sources claim Oric knew about that proposal. The subject of Oric wasn't discussed for very long. Mehovic claimed that Izetbegovic referred to his meeting with Clinton. "SPEAKER: Alija told us about Clinton's offer to have the Chetniks enter Srebrenica and that a military intervention would follow. He asked what we thought about that. We rejected this proposal because we thought that this was outrageous, to murder 5.000 persons. "SPEAKER: However, the idea of Clinton proposing that Serb troops attack Srebrenica and carry out a massacre to justify military intervention seemed utterly ludicrous, but the UN investigation shows Hakija's words are not unfounded. "SPEAKER: UN report delegation have stated that President Izetbegovic also told them that he had learned that a NATO intervention in Bosnia and Herzegovina was possible but could only occur if the Serbs were to break into Srebrenica. "SPEAKER: President Izetbegovic denied having made any such remark. He did admit he asked for an opinion on the land exchange. "SPEAKER: We then talked about an exchange. He offered to replace Srebrenica by Vogosca, and we rejected that too. "SPEAKER: Negotiations will include the demand, first of all, that the maps be altered so that the Bosnian republic acquires Muslim areas along the Drina. "SPEAKER: ... episode, the Croatian army attack on the predominantly Serbian Krajina region was yet to come. On August 1st, 1995, Croatian troops launched a massive assault on the Serbian population of the Krajina, sectors north and south. "SPEAKER: It was an operation of about a hundred thousand Croatian military, yes. Tanks, planes, artillery; the works. "SPEAKER: While officially denying any involvement in what the Croatians called Operation Storm, American forces were actively supporting this bloody operation of ethnic cleansing. "SPEAKER: American equipment was used to jam Serbian communications at a critical moment so that command and control, at least in the communications sector, was blocked and then there was a documented pair of raids on Serbian Krajina military facilities by US navy planes flying out of Aviano which knocked out radar and other facilities. "SPEAKER: The shelling of Knin was a deliberate terror bombardment meant to hasten the departure of the remaining Serbs and was, you know, committed against an unarmed populace. They had street cleaners coming in and removing any evidence of the murders or the vandalism before they brought the cameras in to show the triumphant return of the Croats into Knin. So it was all very carefully planned. "SPEAKER: Having denounced ethnic cleansing, American military planners helped Croatia carry out the largest ethnic cleansing of the war up to that point. "SPEAKER: It would appear to be the largest single incident if you count people affected in the first few days. It was 170.000 people. "SPEAKER: That number quickly grew to 200.000 as a river of humanity clogged the roads. Recently retired US General Charles Boyd Deputy Commander of NATO, confirmed that the US helped plan and implement the attack. "SPEAKER: Croatia would not have taken its military offensives that it has taken, either in Sector West or throughout the north and south, throughout the Krajina, without explicit approval of the US government. "SPEAKER: Roger Cohen of the New York Times quoted a Croatian military journalist who confirmed that General Vuono, of MPRI, met with his Croatian counterpart repeatedly in the days preceding Operation Storm. "SPEAKER: The tactics that they employed when they attack into the Krajina was exactly the same tactics that were used during Desert Storm. They were from American doctrine, attacking on many fronts with lightning-type attacks, and interestingly enough, the Croatian attack was called not Desert Storm but was called Storm. "SPEAKER: The way they deploy and employ their forces is a direct reflection of that training. So it's been very effective and it's been very much a part of the official US policy. "SPEAKER: Canadian UN officers identified an ethnic Albanian commander, Agim Ceku, as responsible for the massacre of Serbian civilians. "SPEAKER: Our officers, Colonel Lesley, General Foran [phoen], that were there on the ground, wanted indictments against the artillery commander in particular, the commander of the operation, and even wanted Tudjman, the Croatian President, indicted for his role. "SPEAKER: Emma Bonino [phoen], Refugee Commissioner for the European Union, noted that as many as 10.000 Serbian civilians were missing from the stream of refugees who fled the Croatian attack on the Krajina. Many of these ended up in mass graves. "SPEAKER: When you go to the villages, you will see the cemeteries, the graves without any names. Mostly it's 90 per cent. "SPEAKER: Sometimes when I'm thinking about what happened there, I think also about the role of the Americans in preparing our army. So I really don't know how they educate our soldiers, but if it is the education for democracy, they look very bad. "SPEAKER: I don't think the American people have drawn that correlation of those incredible war crimes that happened recently in the Krajina and the fact that the Croatian army was trained and advised by and virtually almost led by former American military leadership. "SPEAKER: They have in fact been accomplice to a massive ethnic cleansing of Serbs from Croatia who had lived there for many, many centuries. It was their home. I think we need to step back and be representative of the principle because we only -- not only deny our own principles that way but we create more problems than we solve. "SPEAKER: Three State Department sources told former New York Times reporter David Binder that the green light to undertake Operation Storm came from US envoy Richard Holbrooke, who flew to Zagreb to meet with Croatian President Franjo Tudjman two days before the attack. At first, Holbrooke insisted that he try to prevent Operation Storm, but in his memoir of the Dayton negotiations, Holbrooke acknowledged that he encouraged Operation Storm which drove ethnic Serbs from their homes in the Krajina. "SPEAKER: If you read Holbrooke's memoirs, he writes he was encouraging the Croatian government in every way he could to move fast and hard to get them out. "SPEAKER: Having blocked UN and European peace agreements to end the fighting in Bosnia, the Clinton administration encouraged a joint military offensive by Muslim and Croat forces in Western Bosnia. Like Operation Storm, the offensive was designed to force Serbian civilians from their homes, the very ethnic cleansing the administration had once denounced. In his book 'To End a War', Richard Holbrooke writes that he even advised Croatian forces which Bosnian Serb cities to attack. Those attacks produced nearly as many refugees as Operation Storm and an unknown number of mass graves in Western Bosnia. The following year, after the Dayton Accords were signed, a mass grave of Serbian civilians at Mrkonjic Grad was unearthed. At the time of its discovery in 1996, it was the largest mass grave the war had produced in Bosnia. "With Muslims and Croats on the offensive in Bosnia during the summer and fall of 1995, the US military began to intervene openly against the Serbs. All that was needed was an incident in one of the safe zones. On August 28th, 1995, yet another explosion occurred in the Markale marketplace in Sarajevo, killing scores of innocents and providing a pretext for NATO bombing. "According to the London Times, French and British investigators determined the shell came from Muslim-held positions in Sarajevo, but this time an American officer overruled their finding. "SPEAKER: Now what's significant at this time is exactly within hours after this, NATO, this incredible air armada that was pulled back, cocked, locked, ready to go, the minute this was -- like it was orchestrated in part of a play, this mighty arm of NATO air launched forward and started attacking Serbian positions. They were waiting for that very excuse. "SPEAKER: I have studied Markale I and Markale II for a long time and at the scene and I've talked to a number of people who were involved in the investigations of both, and I am completely persuaded that those two explosions were caused by Muslim forces. "SPEAKER: Bypassing the UN Security Council, which had the legal authority to act in Bosnia, the US had already picked out Bosnian Serb targets, some of them supplied by Muslim commanders. "SPEAKER: We entered the war, took the side of the Muslims and became their air force, bombing the Serbs on this supposed atrocity created by the Serbs where everyone that was on the ground said it was created by the Muslims, which, by the way, is the oldest trick of war. And we fell for it. "SPEAKER: Selective media coverage of the war had created tolerance, if not enthusiasm, for a US military intervention from the American public. "SPEAKER: What amazed me was that American doves, liberals, my allies from the anti-Vietnam days, the sort of people I thought I could count on to oppose reckless American military intervention, were all screaming for military intervention. They were the biggest hawks of all. "SPEAKER: For the Clinton administration, intervention in Bosnia represented a chance to justify the continuation of NATO, an American dominance in Europe. "SPEAKER: NATO's very problem in the early 1990s was simply that the mission for which it was designed had come to an end. It was designed to protect Western Europe from an aggressively expansionist Soviet Yukon. "SPEAKER: The logic would go: You've got to expand NATO, and the only reason to keep and expand NATO is to have a mission. Where is the mission? Bosnia, Balkans. The Balkans had become hostage to an American power concept which is to keep Europe down and America up. "SPEAKER: Senior military officers were amongst those most wary of administration policy. "SPEAKER: I think the mess we have today is a result of political errors. I think we were all too quick to recognise these individual republics as they declared their independence and asked for recognition. We failed to think through the history of this region. And so it's a little -- a little strained to have that political context and then ask the military to go solve the problem."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a lot of original tapes, and it won't present a problem for me to look through them and do that. Now, with respect to international law, in the crisis in Yugoslavia, the sole international legally protected subject was Yugoslavia itself, as a member of the United Nations and the sole bearer of the international legal subjectivity, as a legal subject. So that in that territory, there were no wars. There was just one single war, and that was the war against Yugoslavia. And that war, the fans of that war were flamed [as interpreted] and directed by the greatest power in the modern day world, with reliance on its internal allies, the nationalist, separatist nuclei along with the dominant presence of those forces who were vanquished during World War II. That war used all possible means at its disposal; media, political, military, et cetera. That war, first and foremost, was led by a media campaign that went on for decades. It abused the monopoly over the world information media. Then with a foreign policy intervention which was directed towards the creation of independent states from the Yugoslav -- former Yugoslav republics and the terrible economic campaign against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that can only be qualified as genocide, which went on for many years. And finally, we see the military aggression that took place in 1995 against the Republika Srpska and in the Storm onslaught which we saw a moment ago, along with the participation of NATO forces in the largest possible ethnic cleansing ever recorded, and in 1999 against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia itself. This large-scale media campaign, political, economic, and military campaign to break up Yugoslavia and to restructure the Balkans into new spheres of interest were -- they used manipulations on genocide of Serbs that crowned this false indictment and have great pretentions for it to perform a historical task, and that task being that the basic aim is the last intervention in history. That is to say, through a sort of legal procedure and by legal means to transfer falsehoods and manipulation into the truth. It is necessary for the protagonists of the crimes and those responsible for breaking up Yugoslavia over the decades and who were responsible for the crimes should free them, rid them of their responsibilities and then use this judgement as a historical truth in itself. And that is why I should like to say that this illegal Tribunal, Court, does not exist in a legal framework but exclusively in the media framework, because it in itself represents a means of war and part of the crime that is being perpetuated against the Serbian people. However, this war is being waged with greater or lesser intensity against other peoples as well throughout the world. The victors in the Cold War had said that they are entitled to establish world hegemonism and they've coined that concept; they don't want to make the world a better place to live in, more humane, more legal, but the first post-war decade clearly showed that this was a concept and means to rule over other countries and their natural resources and human resources and that in fact it was a form of new colonialism. And this process that started with the breakdown of the Berlin wall is not a finished process. It is ongoing and is attended by enormous confusion, this sphere of law and legality, history and philosophy, and a new world order is being seen more and more as world chaos, whereas the first post-war Cold War phase has been aborted. These are even assessments by Western experts and the destruction of Yugoslavia ranks among those as well. The messages, such as Clinton's message to the effect that the Serbs were responsible for causing two world wars - that means that the Germans were not responsible for any world war - have the ability to pacify reality and threaten to become a model for shaping the future. This message, launched by the President of America as a world leader - and when I say a world leader, I mean America, not Clinton himself - can be used as a metaphor for a whole decade of a campaign of lies. And I think the only competition to that is what we have been hearing from the opposite party this morning and from the material they have tendered. And that message, the message that I'm talking about, is particularly absurd and unhonourable if we know that it was precisely in those two wars for which, according to Clinton, it was the Serbs who were responsible, it was precisely the Serbs with enormous victims, went hand-in-hand with that same America which was 50 years later to assess that Yugoslavia, and especially Serbia, was standing in its way to realising its new interests and that a free and independent Yugoslavia could not be incorporated into those interests and that with its successful development and freedom-loving spirit, it set a bad example to others and that is why it had to be broken up and turned into a Third World country and, even worse, to send it right back to the Stone Age. And that is why there is nothing more pertinent to the Serbs and Serbia and everybody else, all other freedom-loving people. The great task is to combat lies. And I think that this illegal Tribunal of yours here is quite contrary to the ideas of the people who created it, and despite the restrictions in broadcasting the court process and distorting information, it is part of the decade-long demonisation of the Serbs and a mirror for the perpetrators of crimes against Yugoslavia. This might seem to be paradoxical, but in the historical sense, we have two contradictions here contrary to the ideas of the people that set this Tribunal up. They -- but I would like to have the truth returned to my people and the whole freedom-loving people. This indictment is completely false because in Croatia and in Bosnia it was not a case of aggression but it was a civil war. That is the first point. The second is that in both cases, for the Serb people in Croatia and for the Serb people in Bosnia, it was a defensive war, a war of defence. And a third point according to which the indictment is false both formally and materially is because it accuses Serbs, and I as its president, for the civil war in Croatia and the civil war in Bosnia, whereas Serbia was not at war nor was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at war, either with Croatia or with Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it is precisely the Presidents of Croatia and Bosnia, Tudjman and Izetbegovic, the President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia at the time, Stjepan Mesic, it was they who started this war against Yugoslavia and thereby a war against the Serbs, the citizens of Croatia and the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina first of all by violent means that were contrary to the constitution by an act of secession and then an armed attack against the Serb population. And the violence in Croatia, in fact, began far before independence was ever proclaimed. In this regard, let me say at the outset that I'm not challenging that Serbs helped the Serbs in Bosnia and in Croatia to survive at all. It would -- what is absurd is something that to you seems be logical: That the Americans, the Germans, the Vatican, Iranians, Austria, Turkey, the Afghanistans, et cetera, were helping the Muslims and Croats, but it was not logical to your mind for the Serbs to help Serbs survive on their own threshold, in front of their own front door. We heard here that we financed and helped the Serbs. The Serbs helping the Serbs. And that seems to be a crime. Why, then, is it not a crime that, for example, the Vatican provided money through the Vatican bank for the purchase of weapons for Croatia, by the same token? And then, as Serbia helped the Serbs, I am a criminal, and as the Vatican helped the Croats to perform secession by violent means, the Pope remains the Holy Father. And we helped them to prevent a repeat of the genocide that was conducted over the Serbs in that same region during World War II by those same forces but under the auspices of Hitler and Mussolini during that time, when we saw three Ustashas, for example, taking thousands of Serbs to be slaughtered without anybody standing up to them. And in this regard, both Serbia and I personally invested all my powers and strength in achieving peace, and that is why I said that this particular indictment -- I said this several months ago when you opened the trial, that it was absurd, because Serbia and I myself deserve recognition for working for peace in the area and not as a protagonist of war. Therefore, in view of the fact that Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was not a party in the civil war, not even conceptually or legally or de facto can it be accused of something that went on there. The Security Council ultimately was the sole organ to secure peace and security in the world and assessments about this were not voiced in any of its resolutions or any decisions or public stance with regard to the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina nor did it name the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as the aggressor. It did not point to Yugoslavia as the aggressor. On the other hand, for example, on the 4th of February, 1994, the Security Council adopted a precedential statement cautioning Croatia that it will have to take the consequences unless it withdraws its military units from Bosnia-Herzegovina within the space of two weeks, and then condemnation of Chancellor Kohl who says Croatia promised not to intervene militarily but it did not keep its promise and that is a scandal that we must condemn. So those were the condemnations. They were verbal in character whereas Yugoslavia, although without any foundations whatsoever, was exposed to sanctions, and of course military intervention in the long run and ultimately, whereas the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina started at the time when a majorisation was conducted and a rump referendum accepted. You heard what Lord Carrington had to say about independence. It was held without the Serbian people, despite the fact that the constitution in Bosnia-Herzegovina did not stand, and that that republic was formed for three constituent peoples.
